excerpt: What each part does, how to switch it on safely, how to move the pointer, and how to type your first words. A plain first lesson for anyone who has never used a computer.

body.text: This lesson teaches you the parts of a computer, how to switch it on, and how to type your first words. By the end you will be able to sit at a machine you have never used and do something useful with it. Nothing in this lesson can damage the computer.

A computer has four parts you can see. The tower, or the laptop body, is the machine that stores your work and does the thinking. The monitor is the screen that shows what the machine is doing. The keyboard is how you type. The mouse is how you point. Learn these four names first, because every later lesson uses them.

body.alt: A desktop computer on a wooden desk with a monitor, keyboard and mouse.
body.caption: The four parts: machine, monitor, keyboard, mouse. Check the cables at the back before you blame the computer.

body.text: What you need

items: A desktop computer or a laptop with its charger.
A wall socket that is switched on.
Thirty minutes with no hurry.
Permission to use the machine, if it is not yours.

body.text: Check the cables first

Most computers that look dead are simply disconnected. Before you press anything, look at the back of the machine and follow each cable with your eyes. The monitor needs one cable for power and one cable to the machine. The mouse and keyboard need a cable each or, if they are wireless, batteries that still work.

Start at the wall socket and work inward. Push every plug in gently but firmly. If a plug does not fit the hole, it is the wrong hole. Never force it. A socket that is switched off at the wall looks exactly like a broken computer.
Switch it on
The power button is round. It usually has a small circle with a line through the top. On a laptop it sits above the keyboard. On a desktop tower it sits on the front panel.

items: Press the power button once and take your finger away.
Wait while the machine starts. You may hear a fan, then see the maker's logo.
Do not press the button again. Starting can take twenty seconds or more.
Stop when you reach a sign-in screen or the desktop.

body.text: A password box may appear. If the computer is not yours, ask the owner before you type anything. Guessing can lock the account and cost the owner a repair. If the machine is yours and has no password, click Sign in or your picture to continue.

The desktop is the screen you land on. It shows a picture, a few small icons, and a bar of buttons. Every program you open appears in a window on top of it, and you can close that window without closing the machine.
Move the pointer without fear

Put your hand on the mouse with your wrist resting on the desk. Slide it slowly and watch the small arrow on the screen. That arrow is called the pointer. On a laptop, the pointer moves when you slide one finger on the smooth rectangle below the keyboard. That rectangle is the trackpad.

Keep your wrist on the desk and slide. When you reach the edge of the desk, lift the mouse, set it back in the middle, and keep going. The pointer stays still while the mouse is in the air. That one fact saves beginners months of frustration.

A click is one press and release of the left button. A double-click is two quick clicks in the same spot. Use a double-click on an icon to open it. If nothing opens, you clicked too slowly. Try again faster, without moving the mouse between the clicks.
A right-click opens a short menu with extra actions. It is not an error. Click once on an empty space to close it.

body.alt: A right hand resting on a computer mouse beside a keyboard.
body.caption: Rest your hand on the mouse. One press of the left button is a click. Two quick presses open a file or a program.

body.text: Type your first words
You will type in a program called Notepad on Windows, or TextEdit on a Mac. Both open a plain white page with nothing to distract you, which is exactly what a first lesson needs.

items: On Windows, press the Windows key, type Notepad, then press Enter.
On a Mac, press Command and Space, type TextEdit, then press Enter.
Click once inside the white page. A blinking line appears. That line is the cursor, and your next letter lands there.
Type your full name slowly. Use the long bar at the bottom for a space.
Press Enter to start a new line. Press Backspace to remove the letter before the cursor.
Close the window with the X in the corner. If it asks about saving, choose Don't Save. Saving is the next lesson.

body.text: The letters on the keyboard are not in alphabetical order. They follow an old layout called QWERTY, and almost every keyboard sold here uses it. Today, find your letters one at a time. Speed is a later lesson.
If it goes wrong

items: The screen stays black: check the monitor's power light, the wall socket, and the cable at the back.
The pointer does not move: check the mouse cable, or turn the mouse over and look for a light. A wireless mouse may need new batteries.
Every letter comes out in capitals: Caps Lock is on. Press it once and look for the small light on the key.
The screen is too dark: find the brightness key with a sun symbol, usually on the top row.
The machine ignores everything: hold the power button for ten seconds to switch it off, wait, then press it once to start again.
A message asks for a password you do not have: stop and call the owner. Do not install anything a message tells you to install.

body.text: Practice

items: Name the four parts of the machine out loud, without looking back at this page.
Move the pointer to each corner of the screen and back to the middle.
Open Notepad and type your name, your town, and today's date.
Close the program without saving. Open it again and type the same line, faster.
Switch off properly: open the Start menu, click the power symbol, then choose Shut down.

body.text: You can now start a computer, read the desktop, move the pointer, click, and type. In the next lesson you will learn where your work is kept, so that nothing you type has to disappear again.

excerpt: A file is one document. A folder holds files. Learn where your work is kept, how to save it under a name you will still understand later, and how to find it again.

body.text: This lesson shows you where your work lives after you type it. You will learn what a file is, what a folder is, how to save with a clear name, and how to find the file again. Read it once, then do the steps on a real computer.

A file is one complete piece of work. It can be a letter, a picture, a form, or a song. A folder is a container that holds files. Folders can sit inside other folders, and that is how a computer keeps thousands of documents in order without losing any of them.

body.alt: A file window showing the Documents, Pictures and Desktop folders.
body.caption: Each yellow icon is a folder. Double-click a folder to open it, and look at the address bar at the top to see where you are.

body.text: The folders you already have

Open File Explorer on Windows, the yellow folder icon on the taskbar, or Finder on a Mac. You will see the same main folders. They are not decoration. Each one has a job, and using the right one is most of the work.

items: Desktop: things you are using today. Easy to reach, and easy to fill with clutter.
Documents: letters, forms, school work, and anything you write.
Pictures: photographs and saved images.
Downloads: files the internet sends you. Treat it as a delivery mat, not a store room.
Recycle Bin or Trash: files you deleted. They stay there until you empty it.

body.text: Make one folder for each part of your life

A good folder structure answers one question fast: where would I look for this in six months? Keep it shallow. Three levels are enough for most people, and deep nests of folders hide files from the person who made them.

items: Open Documents.
Right-click an empty space, choose New, then Folder.
Type a name such as School and press Enter.
Open School and make folders inside it, such as Fees and Certificates.
Do the same once for Work and once for Personal.
Stop there. You can add folders later when you need them.

body.text: Use names you would say out loud. A folder called Misc feels tidy on the day you make it. By December it is useless, because you cannot remember what you hid inside.
Save a file where you can find it
Until you save, your work exists only in the open window. If the light goes, it is gone. Saving copies the work onto the disk, where it stays with the machine switched off.

items: Type one sentence in Word, Notepad, or Google Docs.
Press Ctrl and S together. On a Mac, press Command and S.
The first time, the computer asks for a name and a place. This is the most important minute of the work.
Choose Documents, then the folder you made.
Name the file with the subject and the month, for example school-fees-march-2026.
Press Save.

body.text: A name like Document (3) tells you nothing next month. A name with the subject, the place, and the date tells you everything, even when you are tired and hunting for it at midnight.
Save again, and save a copy
From now on, Ctrl and S updates the same file without asking questions. Press it every few minutes while you write. If the power goes, you lose the last minute, not the afternoon.

Save As makes a new copy under a new name. Use it when you want to keep the old version and start a new one. For example, save school-fees-march, then use Save As to create school-fees-april. Avoid final, final2, and latest-final, because none of them tells a reader which one is true.

body.alt: A desk with a laptop, a notebook and a pen beside it.
body.caption: Write the file name in your notebook for the first month. A name you can read back is a file you can find again.

body.text: If the file is missing

items: Look in Documents, then inside the folder you remember using.
Open the Recycle Bin or Trash. Deleted files stay there until you empty it. Right-click the file and choose Restore.
Use the search box at the top of File Explorer or Finder, and type part of the name you gave it.
Check Downloads. Many files are saved there without the person noticing.
Open the program and look at its list of recent files, which usually sits on the first screen.

body.text: Practice

items: Make a folder called Practice inside Documents.
Write a short note, save it inside Practice as my-first-file, then close it.
Open the file from File Explorer, add one sentence, and press Ctrl and S.
Delete the file, then restore it from the Recycle Bin.
Search for the file by typing part of its name, and open it from the results.

body.text: You can now save work so that it survives a power cut, and find it again months later. The next lesson teaches your hands to type without hunting for every key.

excerpt: Where to rest your fingers, which keys fix mistakes, and the shortcuts that save hours. Ten minutes of practice a day is enough to stop hunting for letters.

body.text: This lesson teaches you to type without hunting for every key. You will learn where to rest your fingers, how to fix mistakes quickly, and the shortcuts you will use every day. Ten minutes of practice is enough to improve.

Typing is a physical skill, like riding a bicycle. Reading about it does not make you faster. Do the steps on a real keyboard, slowly, and your hands will learn the positions on their own. Speed comes from accuracy, not from force.
Sit and place your hands
Before you type a word, set up your body. A bad position is why many people blame the computer for back and wrist pain after an hour of work.

items: Sit upright with both feet flat on the floor.
Keep the screen at eye level, about an arm's length away.
Bend your elbows at about ninety degrees and keep your shoulders down.
Rest the four fingers of your left hand on A, S, D, and F.
Rest the four fingers of your right hand on J, K, L, and the key beside L.
Rest both thumbs on the long bar at the bottom.

body.text: Feel the small raised line on the F and J keys. Those two bumps let you find your place without looking down. The eight keys under your fingers are called the home row, and every other key is reached from there.

body.alt: Two hands resting on a laptop keyboard in the home row position.
body.caption: Left fingers on A, S, D, F. Right fingers on J, K, L and the key beside L. Thumbs on the space bar.

body.text: The keys that edit, not just write
Most mistakes at the beginning come from pressing the wrong editing key, not from a broken machine. These are the ones worth knowing on the first day.

items: Enter or Return finishes a line and starts a new one.
Backspace removes the letter before the cursor.
Delete removes the letter after the cursor, or deletes a selected item.
Space bar leaves one space between words. Press it once, not three times.
Shift gives a capital letter, or the symbol printed above a number key.
Caps Lock types every letter in capitals until you press it again.
Tab jumps to the next box in a form, or indents a line.

body.text: If every letter comes out in capitals, Caps Lock is on. A small light on the key itself usually shows it, though some laptops show it on the screen instead. Press the key once and continue typing. If you did not look, press Ctrl and Z to undo the capitals.
Five shortcuts that save time
A shortcut is two keys pressed together. It does the same job as a menu, with fewer steps and without moving your hand to the mouse.

items: Ctrl and C copies what you selected.
Ctrl and V pastes the copy where the cursor is.
Ctrl and X cuts, which moves the selection instead of copying it.
Ctrl and Z undoes your last action. It is the most forgiving key on the computer.
Ctrl and S saves the file.

body.text: On a Mac, use Command in place of Ctrl. The letters stay the same, so Command and C copies and Command and Z undoes. To select text, click at the start of a word, hold the button down, and drag to the end. The text changes colour, and then the shortcut can act on it.

body.alt: A learner typing on a laptop with a document open on the screen.
body.caption: Select first, then copy. The text turns a different colour when the computer knows what you mean.

body.text: If it goes wrong

items: Letters appear in the wrong place: you clicked somewhere else in the text. Click where you want the cursor, or press Ctrl and Z.
Every letter is a capital: press Caps Lock once.
A key repeats and fills the line: the key is stuck. Press it firmly a few times, or switch the keyboard.
The cursor jumps while you type: your palm is touching the laptop trackpad. Move your hands back or turn the trackpad off.
You typed a whole line into the wrong box: select it, press Ctrl and X, click the right box, and press Ctrl and V.
Your wrists ache: stop for the day, raise the chair or the screen, and keep your wrists straight.

body.text: Practice

items: Type the home row letters, left hand then right hand, ten times without looking down.
Type your full name ten times, using Shift for each capital letter.
Type a sentence, press Ctrl and Z twice, then type it again.
Write the same short sentence for ten minutes a day for one week.
At the end of the week, count how many mistakes you make. Aim to make fewer, not to type faster.

body.text: You can now find the home row by touch, fix a mistake without panic, and use the shortcuts that most office work depends on. The next lesson shows you how to reach the internet and find what you need without getting lost.

excerpt: How to open a browser, tell the address bar from the search box, use tabs, read a web address, and save a page you will want again. Simple habits that prevent most mistakes.

body.text: This lesson teaches you to use the internet on purpose. You will open a browser, search for what you need, keep pages open in tabs, and check that a site is really the one you wanted.

The internet is a very large library with no librarian and no locked door. Anyone can put a page on the shelf, including people who want your password or your money. The skills in this lesson are mostly about knowing which shelf you are standing at.
Open the browser and read the screen
The browser is the program you use to visit pages. The common ones are Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Safari. They all work the same way, so learning one is enough.

items: Click the browser icon on the taskbar, or search for Chrome or Edge in the Start menu.
Find the long box at the top. That is the address bar.
Type an address you know, such as cea.ng, and press Enter.
Read the address after the page loads, and check it is the place you asked for.
Use the left arrow at the top left to go back one page.

body.text: The address bar can also search. If you type two or three words it does not recognise, it will send them to a search engine. That is convenient and it is also how people arrive somewhere they did not intend to go.

body.alt: A young man searching on a laptop at a small table with a phone beside him.
body.caption: The address bar is the top box. Read it before you trust a page, because it shows the real owner of the site.

body.text: Ask a search engine a real question

A search works when the question is specific. Computer is a warehouse. How to save a Word document on Windows 11 is a shelf. Put the thing you want and the situation you are in into the same sentence.

Add the word Nigeria when the answer depends on where you are, for example JAMB registration deadline Nigeria. Read the grey address under each result before you click it. A result from waec.org.ng is not the same as a blog that mentioned WAEC once.

The first results are often adverts, marked Ad or Sponsored. They can still be useful, but they paid to be there. Scroll until you see results that are not marked, and open the one that seems to answer your question. If it is wrong, press Back and try another. Back is the most forgiving button on the internet.
Use tabs instead of losing your place
A tab is a page you keep open while you look at another. The row of small titles at the top of the browser is the tab bar, and the plus sign opens a new one.

items: Click the plus sign to open a new tab.
Type a different address or search in the new tab.
Click a tab title to switch back to that page.
Click the small X on a tab to close only that page.
Right-click a closed space on the tab bar and choose Reopen closed tab if you closed one by mistake.

body.text: Closing the whole browser window closes every tab in it. Closing one tab closes only that page. Keep the number of tabs small, or you will spend more time looking for a page than reading it.
Check a site before you trust it
A small padlock beside the address means the connection is private, so other people on the network cannot read what you send. It does not mean the owner is honest. A thief can rent a padlock too.

items: Read the address slowly and look for spelling tricks, such as gtbank-help.com instead of gtbank.com.
If the browser shows a red warning that the connection is not private, do not type a password there.
If a page asks for your bank details and you arrived from a link in a message, close it and type the bank address yourself.
If a page tells you your computer is infected, close the tab. That message is usually an advert for a fake repair.
If a download starts without asking, close the tab and check your Downloads folder before opening anything.

body.text: Keep the pages you will need again

Downloads land in your Downloads folder. Move the file into Documents if you mean to keep it, the way you would carry a parcel off the floor. Bookmarks are saved addresses: click the star at the end of the address bar, give it a name you will recognise, and open it later from Bookmarks.

body.alt: A laptop on a desk showing a browser with several tabs open.
body.caption: Five bookmarks you use every week are worth more than fifty you saved and forgot.

body.text: If it goes wrong

items: The page will not load: check the Wi-Fi or data connection, then press the reload button once.
You cannot find a page you had open: right-click the tab bar and choose Reopen closed tab.
Every page is slow: close the tabs you are not using, then try again.
A page is asking for money or a card: leave it, and reach the organisation through its official address.
You downloaded something by accident: open Downloads, delete the file, and do not open it first.

body.text: Practice

items: Open your browser and type cea.ng in the address bar.
Open two more tabs and search for a word you need to look up today.
Use Back to return to the first result list, then switch tabs by clicking the titles.
Save the page you use most often as a bookmark.
Check the address of every page you open for the next ten minutes before you type anything into it.

body.text: You can now reach a page, search for what you need, keep several pages open, and check where you actually are. The next lesson uses those skills to send your first email.

excerpt: An address, a subject that tells the truth, a short body with one job, and the paperclip. How to write and send a first email that a school or office will answer.

body.text: This lesson teaches you to send an email that looks like a person wrote it on purpose. You will learn the parts of an address, how to fill To, Subject, and the message, and how to attach a file. You will also learn when to use Reply and when to use Reply all.

Email is a letter that arrives in seconds. WhatsApp is faster, but schools, banks, and employers still ask for email because it keeps a record. A message sent by email can be found a year later, along with the file that came with it.

body.alt: A laptop showing an email being written with To, Subject and a message body.
body.caption: Three fields decide whether the mail works: To, Subject, and the body. Read all three before you press Send.

body.text: Read your own address first

An email address has two parts around the @ sign. The part before it is the name you chose. The part after it is the provider, such as gmail.com, outlook.com, or cea.ng. Your address is your name on the internet, so treat it like one.
Write your address in a notebook now. People lose work because they forget their own address, create a second one, and then check the wrong inbox. One address, written down, is enough for years.
Fill the three fields in order

Open Gmail, Outlook, or the Mail app and click Compose or New mail. A blank message appears with fields at the top. Fill them from the top down, so you never send a finished letter to the wrong person.

items: To: type the other person's address exactly. One wrong letter sends the mail to a stranger or to nobody.
Subject: write the short label the reader will see in a list of fifty. Application for Computer Basics, September is a subject. Hello is not.
Body: click the large empty space and write the letter.
Check the address and the subject once more before you type a single word.

body.text: A body that works here and anywhere else has four parts. Greet the person by name. Say in one sentence why you are writing. Say in one sentence what you want them to do. End with your full name and a phone number. That is enough. Do not write in capitals. If you need four answers, do not put four questions in one mail, because people reply to the last one and forget the rest.
Send a practice mail

items: Open Gmail or Outlook in the browser.
Click Compose.
Put a trusted address in To, such as a family member or a second address of your own.
Subject: Practice mail from your name.
Body: Good morning. This is a practice message. My name is your name. My number is your number.
Click Send, then open the other inbox and confirm the mail arrived.

body.text: If the mail does not arrive within a minute, open the Sent folder. If it is there, the address was accepted. Then check the Spam or Junk folder of the receiving account before you send it again.
Attach a file correctly
An attachment is a file that travels with the letter: a receipt, a passport photograph, a filled form. Look for the paperclip icon on the compose window and click it.

items: Choose the file from Documents, Desktop, or Downloads.
Wait until the file name appears under the body, or a small box shows the upload finished.
Check the name. school-fees.pdf tells the reader what it is. IMG_0048 tells them nothing.
Send a PDF when the file is a document, so it looks the same on the other person's computer.
Keep the file under about 10 MB where you can. A photo straight from a phone camera is often larger than that.

body.text: If you write Please find attached, look under the body first. A mail that promises a file and carries nothing wastes a day, and the reader will not always tell you.

body.alt: An email with a paperclip attachment showing a PDF named school-fees.pdf.
body.caption: The paperclip means a file is coming. Check that the name is there before you press Send.

body.text: Reply, Reply all, and Forward

items: Reply sends your answer to the person who wrote to you.
Reply all sends it to everyone who received the original, which is wrong when thirty parents are on the list.
Forward sends the letter to a new person. Add one sentence at the top saying why you are forwarding it.
Use Reply by default, and use Reply all only when every person on the list needs your answer.

body.text: If it goes wrong

items: The mail bounces back: one letter in the address is wrong. Compare it with the address the person gave you.
The attachment will not send: the file is too large. Send a link, or make the photo or PDF smaller.
You sent the mail to the wrong person: email cannot be recalled. Write again at once and say what happened.
The reply does not come: wait a day, check Spam, then send a short follow-up rather than five repeats.
A stranger asks you to confirm a password by email: do not reply. No bank asks for a password by email.

body.text: Practice

items: Write your own address on paper and read it aloud to somebody.
Send a practice mail to a trusted address with a clear subject and your full name.
Attach one PDF or photograph to a second mail and check the name appears before you send.
Open your Spam folder and look at what a fake bank message looks like, without clicking anything inside it.

body.text: You can now write an email that is easy to answer, attach the right file, and avoid the two mistakes that embarrass people most. The next lesson is about the passwords that protect all of this.
